sermon:
## The Word Became Flesh: How the Infinite God Moved Into the Neighborhood (John 1:1–18)
*Why the incarnation is not a doctrine to admire from a distance but a person who took a body you could touch*

**Text:** John 1:1–18 · **Supporting:** Genesis 1:1 · Exodus 40:34–35 · Colossians 1:15–17 · Philippians 2:6–8 · Hebrews 1:1–3 · 1 John 1:1

Most of us have made our peace with a God who stays back. A first cause behind the machinery. A silence with good manners. A power we would rather not have looking at us too closely. We call it reverence, but a good deal of it is relief. A God at that distance cannot embarrass us at dinner or follow us into the room where we are worst. John opens his Gospel by taking that God away from us. He does not argue us out of our distance. He tells us God ended it Himself.

### I. In the Beginning Was the Word: The One Through Whom Everything Was Made (John 1:1–5)

John does not begin with a manger. He begins before the world. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Every Jew reading that first phrase heard it land on top of another one. Genesis 1:1: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." John is writing a second Genesis on purpose, and he is telling you who was there in the first.

The word he chose is *logos*. To a Greek it meant the rational order holding the cosmos together, the logic under all things, the principle a philosopher spent his life trying to reach. To a Jew steeped in the prophets it meant the word of the Lord that came to Isaiah and Jeremiah, the word that does not return void, the word that spoke light out of nothing in the first line of the Bible. Two civilizations had been reaching, from opposite directions, for the thing that held everything together. John takes both of their reachings and drives them into one person. The reason the universe hangs together is not a principle. It is a person. And that person was with God, and was God, and was not made, "all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3).

John says three things about the Word in one breath, and he needs all three. The Word *was*, He did not begin; He is eternal. The Word was *with* God, He is distinct, a person you can be with, face to face. And the Word *was* God, He is not a lesser thing near God but God Himself. Take away any one and the sentence collapses into a heresy the church would spend centuries refusing. Leave all three and you have the mystery the whole Gospel will unfold: the God who was always there, the God you can stand beside, the God who is fully God, walking into His own creation on human feet.

- **A. The Word is the agent of creation, not a creature within it.** Paul says the same thing in Colossians 1:16–17: "by him were all things created… and by him all things consist." Consist, *sunistēmi*, held together. The atoms in your hand are not self-managing. Every second, something holds them. John and Paul both name Him. Nothing you can see made itself, and the One who made it all was not made.
- **B. The light shines in a darkness that could not master it.** "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not" (John 1:5). That word, *katalambanō*, means both to understand and to overcome. The darkness did not understand the light and could not put it out. John writes his whole Gospel under that sentence. The cross is coming. The tomb is coming. The darkness will do its worst to the light. It will not win.

### II. The Word Was Made Flesh and Dwelt Among Us: The Scandal of the Incarnation (John 1:6–18)

Then the sentence the ancient world found impossible. "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory" (John 1:14). *Sarx.* Flesh. Not that God appeared to have a body, not that He wore humanity like a costume He could remove. The Word became flesh. To a Greek philosopher this was not merely strange but offensive. The whole point of the divine was that it stayed clean of matter, above the mess, untouched. John says the untouchable One took on a body that got tired, wept, bled, and died.

Look at the verb "dwelt." *Skēnoō*, He pitched His tent, He tabernacled among us. Every Jewish reader knew the tabernacle. In Exodus 40:34–35 the glory of the Lord filled the tent so densely that "Moses was not able to enter into the tent of the congregation, because the cloud abode thereon, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." That is the whole history of the covenant in one image, God with His people, but behind a veil, in a tent, at a distance you did not cross and live. Even Moses could not walk in. John says the glory has moved. It is no longer in the tent behind the veil. It is in the man they could walk up to and touch. "And we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14).

Read that phrase slowly, *full of grace and truth*. Those are covenant words. In Exodus 34, when the glory passes before Moses, the Lord proclaims Himself "abundant in goodness and truth." John is telling you that the character that thundered on Sinai now has a human face, and it did not lose an ounce of its glory by coming close. We assume that intimacy must mean the loss of majesty, that a God near enough to touch must be a God shrunk down. John says the opposite. They beheld His glory precisely in the flesh. The nearness was not the dilution of the glory. It was the fullest display of it.

- **A. He came to His own, and His own received Him not.** "He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not. He came unto his own, and his own received him not" (John 1:10–11). The One through whom the world was made walked into it, and the world looked at its Maker and saw a laborer from Nazareth. This is the oldest human failure. We do not recognize the hand that holds us up. But John will not leave it there: "But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name" (John 1:12). The fatherless are given a Father. The unmade are born.
- **B. No man has seen God, except the Son has told Him out.** "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (John 1:18). *Exēgēsato*, He has told the Father out, exposited Him in flesh. This is why Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the express image of his person." John says you cannot see God. Then he says: look at Jesus. If you want to know what God is like when He is not managing His reputation, watch Him touch a leper. The invisible God has an audible voice and a face that wept.

### III. Living Well When You No Longer Expect God to Come Close

We say we want a God who keeps His distance, and then we are furious that He seems so far. We have arranged both. We built the theology that keeps Him back, a designer, a force, a value system, a mood, and then we grieve the silence we engineered. I have preached a manageable God. I have handed people a God-shaped principle when they were dying for a God-shaped person, because the principle asks nothing of me and the person asks everything. John will not let us keep it. He says the distance is over, and the ending of it is not comfortable, because a God who moves in next door can see how you actually live.

The early church understood the stakes and fought for this one sentence for four hundred years. At the Council of Nicaea in 325, against a teacher named Arius who insisted the Son was a created being, however exalted, the church refused to shave a hair off John 1:1. The word they would not surrender was *homoousios*, of one substance with the Father. Not similar. The same. A century later, at Chalcedon in 451, they refused the opposite error too, that His humanity was a costume, that the flesh was less than real, and confessed Him fully God and fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion and without division. It reads like theological hair-splitting from a distance. It is not. They saw what we keep trying to forget: a Christ who is only a great teacher cannot save you, and a Christ who only seemed human never touched your actual life. Both errors leave you exactly where you started, alone, unmade, unreached. The whole gospel rides on the word John gave them. The Word was flesh.

- **A. A distant God cannot reach the room where you are worst.** The reason people prefer the far-off God is that His distance protects their privacy. A first cause behind the machine will never ask about your marriage. A cosmic force has no opinion on how you treat your children. But a God who will not come close also cannot come to the hospital corridor at 2 a.m., the argument that ends the marriage, the grave you stand beside not knowing what you believe anymore. The tent-God stayed behind the veil, and behind the veil He could not hold your hand. John 1:14 is the end of the veil. He pitched His tent in the middle of the mess, the poverty, the political violence, the family that thought He was out of His mind, and the glory did not dim for the closeness. It was still the glory. Full of grace and truth.
- **B. Christ is the only exegesis of God we have.** Every other picture of God you carry, the disappointed father, the cosmic accountant, the indifferent physics, the god who is mostly your own conscience wearing a robe, is a guess made in the dark. And we are all making the guess. The atheist guesses there is no one there; the vague believer guesses there is someone benign; both are guessing, because "no man hath seen God at any time" (John 1:18). But John says there is one exception. There is one who has been in the bosom of the Father and came back to tell us, and He told us not in a lecture but in a life you can read straight through. If your God does not look like Jesus, your God is not the one who made you. He came unto His own, and His own received Him not. The question John hands you is whether you will be His own who does.

The Word moved into the neighborhood.

## Born Again: Why You Do Not Need Improvement but a New Birth (John 3)
*What Jesus told the best religious man in Jerusalem in the dark*

**Text:** John 3 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 36:25–27 · Numbers 21:8–9 · Titus 3:5 · 1 Peter 1:3 · 2 Corinthians 5:17 · Romans 8:7–8

A man came to Jesus at night. He was not a beggar or a leper or a tax collector. He was Nicodemus, a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, a member of the Sanhedrin, the top of the religious order, the man other men measured themselves against. If anyone had earned the right to a straight conversation with God, it was this man. And Jesus, before Nicodemus can finish his opening compliment, tells him he has to start over. Not improve. Start over. Be born. The best man in the city needed the one thing his goodness could not buy.

### I. Except a Man Be Born Again: The Diagnosis Nicodemus Did Not Expect (John 3:1–8)

Nicodemus opens with respect. "Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him" (John 3:2). It is a generous, careful, orthodox thing to say. Jesus does not thank him for it. "Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3). The word is *anōthen*, it means both *again* and *from above*. Nicodemus hears only "again" and stumbles into the absurd: "How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?" (John 3:4).

Jesus is not talking about biology. He is talking about a birth that comes from above, from God, from outside you altogether. "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" (John 3:5–6). Flesh produces flesh. Effort produces effort. A moral man produces a more moral man. But no amount of flesh has ever produced spirit, any more than a river ever ran uphill on its own.

Watch how gently and how firmly Jesus dismantles him. Nicodemus has spent his whole life on the assumption that a man draws near to God by rising, more study, more law-keeping, more scrupulous obedience, a ladder of righteousness climbed rung by rung. It is the most respectable assumption in the world, and it is the one Jesus takes away first. You cannot climb into a birth. Birth is not something the infant accomplishes; it is something that happens to the infant. By choosing that image Jesus is telling the most accomplished religious man in Jerusalem that his entire method, the ladder, the effort, the upward reach, was aimed at a door that does not open from the outside. The kingdom is not scaled. It is entered, and only by those who were carried in.

- **A. The kingdom is entered by birth, not by achievement.** You did not contribute to your first birth. You were not consulted. You did not assist. You were the one thing that happened to you and never the one who arranged it. Jesus reaches for that image on purpose. The new birth is not the crown on a life of religious effort. It is a thing done to you by Another, and your part is the part a newborn plays.
- **B. The Spirit blows where He wills, and you did not schedule Him.** "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit" (John 3:8). In both Hebrew and Greek the word for wind and the word for spirit are the same, *ruach*, *pneuma*. You cannot manage the wind. You cannot manufacture the Spirit. Ezekiel already promised it: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you… and I will put my spirit within you" (Ezekiel 36:26–27). I will. Not you.

### II. As Moses Lifted Up the Serpent: How the New Birth Is Bought (John 3:9–21)

Nicodemus is still lost. "How can these things be?" (John 3:9). Jesus takes him back into his own Scriptures, to a story every Pharisee had memorized. In Numbers 21 the people of Israel are dying of snakebite in the wilderness, and God tells Moses to lift a bronze serpent on a pole. "And it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live" (Numbers 21:8). No medicine. No striving. No climbing to reach it. Look, and live.

"And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life" (John 3:14–15). Jesus tells Nicodemus in the dark how the new birth will be paid for. Someone will be lifted up on a pole. The people bitten by the ancient serpent, dying of the venom in their own flesh, will be told to do the one thing pride hates most, stop working, and look.

Notice what the bronze serpent required of the dying Israelite: nothing but a turned head. There was no ointment to apply, no ritual to complete, no distance to cross. A man too far gone to walk could still turn his eyes. A child could do it. That is the offense of it to a man like Nicodemus, whose whole identity was built on being able to do what ordinary men could not. The cure God provides is so simple it insults our competence. And it must be, because the people it saves are past the point of competence. They are dying. The venom is already in them. The only strength required is the strength to look at what God has lifted up, which is to say, no strength of theirs at all.

- **A. The new birth is not earned by the looker; it is bought by the lifted-up One.** Then the verse the whole world half-remembers. "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life" (John 3:16). We have printed it on so much that we have forgotten it is about a man on a pole and a people who are already dying. It is not a warm sentiment. It is an emergency rescue described with terrible tenderness.
- **B. The judgment is not that God is harsh, but that men loved the dark.** "And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil" (John 3:19). The problem was never that the light was too dim to find. The problem is that light exposes, and we would rather not be seen. Nicodemus came at night. John tells us the hour on purpose.

### III. Living Well When You Have Confused Being Good With Being Alive

The reason this text unsettles the church more than the world is that we are all Nicodemus. We are the churchgoers, the responsible ones, the people who came early and gave and served and believed the right things. And Jesus looks at the best of us and says: none of that is the new birth. I have built ministries that produced better-behaved flesh and called it revival. I have polished people who were never made alive and been proud of the shine. The most dangerous distance from God is not the far country. It is the front pew, improved and unborn.

The eighteenth-century Church of England knew this diagnosis by heart. On the twenty-fourth of May, 1738, a failed missionary named John Wesley, an ordained minister, a moralist so disciplined he ran a society at Oxford that his classmates mocked as the Holy Club, sat in a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London and heard Luther's preface to the Epistle to the Romans read aloud. Wesley had already sailed to the American colony of Georgia to convert the natives and come home a failure, writing in his journal, "I went to America to convert the Indians; but oh, who shall convert me?" He was Nicodemus with a clergy collar. That evening he wrote that his heart was "strangely warmed," and that for the first time he trusted in Christ, "Christ alone," for salvation. Wesley had been religious his whole life. That night he was born. The man who had been trying to save himself by effort discovered that the effort had never once reached the thing effort cannot reach.

- **A. Improvement leaves the self on the throne; the new birth removes it.** Self-improvement is the flesh applying itself to the flesh, and it always ends with a person who is a little better and still in charge. Romans 8:7 says "the carnal mind is enmity against God." You cannot renovate enmity into worship. Paul says the new self is a *creation*: "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new" (2 Corinthians 5:17). Not a repaired thing. A made thing.
- **B. Christ was lifted up so the unborn could look and live.** The connection Jesus drew for Nicodemus is the connection He draws for you. The Son of man was lifted up on a Roman pole outside Jerusalem, and the venom of the ancient serpent that runs in all our veins was answered there. Your part is not to climb, not to improve, not to qualify. Your part is the part the dying Israelites played. Look, and live. Titus 3:5 says He saved us "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy… by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost." Washing. Renewing. Both done to you. And here is the mercy hidden inside the whole hard diagnosis: if the new birth were something you achieved, you could lose it the way you lose everything you achieve. Because it is something done to you from above, it holds when you cannot. Nicodemus came at night. John's last word on him is that he came back for the body of Jesus, in daylight, carrying myrrh and aloes (John 19:39). Somewhere between the two visits, the wind blew. It is still blowing. And it may be blowing on you as you read this, which is the only reason any of these words could reach you at all.

You must be born from above.

## The Woman at the Well: Living Water for the Person Everyone Else Avoided (John 4)
*Why Jesus went out of His way to the one town no respectable rabbi would enter*

**Text:** John 4 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 2:13 · Isaiah 55:1 · Psalm 42:1–2 · John 7:37–38 · Revelation 22:17 · Romans 5:8

There was a shorter road, and Jesus took the longer one on purpose. Every observant Jew traveling from Judea to Galilee crossed the Jordan twice to go around Samaria, because Samaria was unclean and the Samaritans were half-breeds and heretics, and a rabbi did not soil himself with that country. John says "he must needs go through Samaria" (John 4:4). There was no geographical necessity. The necessity was in the heart of God. He went where He did not have to go, to meet a woman no one else would be caught near, at the hottest hour of the day, when the respectable women were home and only the outcast came for water alone.

### I. Give Me to Drink: The God Who Starts at the Bottom (John 4:1–26)

He is tired, and thirsty, and He sits down by Jacob's well at the sixth hour, the blistering noon. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and Jesus says, "Give me to drink" (John 4:7). Three barriers fall in four words. He is a man speaking to a woman alone, which no rabbi did. He is a Jew asking a Samaritan for a favor, which no Jew did. He is a holy man making Himself indebted to a woman the whole town had written off. She is stunned: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans" (John 4:9).

Then He turns her thirst into the subject. "If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water" (John 4:10). She hears plumbing; He means the Spirit. In her world "living water" meant running water, a spring or a river as opposed to the still water of a cistern, and she is standing at a well fed by a spring, so she thinks He is boasting. "Art thou greater than our father Jacob?" (John 4:12). He lets the double meaning do its work. "Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: but whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:13–14).

Hear what He is actually saying to her. Everything you have been drinking to fill this thirst, He is not condemning the water in the well; He is diagnosing the thirst underneath it. Every relationship, every escape, every arrangement she had made to stop the ache had worked for an afternoon and then run dry, which is why she was on husband number six. He is not surprised by this. He is telling her the reason. The thirst she keeps trying to drown was never for any of the things she reached for. It was for God, and no created thing on earth is God-shaped enough to fill it.

- **A. Every human being is at the well because of an inner drought.** Jeremiah named her condition and ours a thousand years earlier: "for my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Two evils. We leave the fountain, and then we dig. She had dug five cisterns and was standing beside a sixth, and every one had leaked dry. The thirst was never about water.
- **B. He exposes her wound not to shame her but to reach it.** "Go, call thy husband, and come hither" (John 4:16). She answers that she has none, and He finishes the sentence for her: "for thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband" (John 4:18). He did not raise it to humiliate her. He raised it because you cannot give living water to a thirst that stays hidden. Isaiah 55:1 had already sent the invitation to exactly this kind of person: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters." Everyone. Especially the one at the noon well, alone.

### II. The Hour Cometh, and Now Is: Worship Larger Than the Mountain (John 4:19–42)

Caught, she does what we all do, she changes the subject to theology. Where should we worship, your mountain or ours? It is the oldest deflection: turn the personal into the abstract before He gets any closer. Jesus does not take the bait, and He does not despise the question either. "But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him" (John 4:23). The mountain is not the point. The Father is seeking. Not being sought. Seeking.

Then, to a Samaritan woman with a ruined reputation, at noon, by a well, He says the thing He hides from nearly everyone else in the Gospel until His trial. She says the Messiah is coming, and when He comes "he will tell us all things" (John 4:25). "Jesus saith unto her, I that speak unto thee am he" (John 4:26). In the Greek it is closer to "I am, the one speaking to you," and the Jewish ear would catch the echo of the divine name from Exodus, the *I AM* that spoke to Moses at the bush. The clearest self-disclosure of His identity in the whole book of John, and He spends it on her. Not on Nicodemus the ruler who came by night. Not on the crowds or the council. On a Samaritan woman with five failed marriages, alone at a well at noon. The Messiah of Israel unveils Himself first to a half-breed heretic the whole town avoided, and He does it because she finally stopped hiding.

- **A. The one nobody chose became the first missionary in Samaria.** She left her waterpot, the thing she came for, now forgotten, and ran to the town that had shunned her. "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" (John 4:29). "And many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman" (John 4:39). The person the town avoided became the reason the town believed. He did not clean her up and send her to training. He met her thirst, and she ran.
- **B. Christ's food was to do the will of the One who sent Him.** The disciples come back with lunch and are baffled that He is not hungry. "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work" (John 4:34). The word *finish*, *teleioō*, is the same root that will hang over the whole Gospel until the cross. The Father seeks; the Son finishes the seeking. Reaching this woman was not a detour from His mission. It was His mission, in one afternoon.

### III. Living Well When You Have Written People Off, and Been Written Off

We have all built a Samaria. A category of people we would rather go around. The addict, the divorced, the one whose sin is loud and public, the tribe we have decided is beyond reach. And here is the harder mirror: we did not only build it around others. We built it around ourselves. Everyone reading this has a noon-well hour, the thing you do alone, when the respectable ones are not watching, because you cannot face them and it. I have gone around the Samaria in my own congregation. I have crossed to the other side of the room from the person whose need embarrassed me. Jesus crossed the whole country toward her.

In 1865, in London's East End, Whitechapel, the poorest, most avoided slum in the empire, thick with drunkenness and prostitution and gin shops, the district polite Christians would not enter, William and Catherine Booth left the respectable pulpit and planted a mission among exactly the people the churches had written off. It grew, and in 1878 it took the name the Salvation Army. They were mocked for it, pelted in the streets, denounced from proper pulpits for dragging the gospel into the gutter. Their whole conviction was that the gospel goes to the noon well, to the drunk and the prostitute and the person no respectable ministry would touch, because that is precisely where the thirst is loudest and the Savior most Himself. They did not wait for the outcasts to become presentable before they were worth the trouble. They went where they did not have to go, into the one part of the city everyone else crossed the river to avoid.

- **A. The living water is offered to your worst hour, not your best.** We keep trying to bring God our polished cistern and hide the broken ones. We come to the well at noon so no one will see how many times we have failed, and then we wonder why the water never satisfies, because we brought Him the version of ourselves that did not need Him. He asks to see the broken ones. He asked her about the husbands. Romans 5:8 says "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Not once we were cleaned up. Not after we became the kind of person a Savior could respectably associate with. While. The woman got the clearest word of who He is in the whole Gospel precisely because she stopped hiding the five failures and the sixth. The exposure was not the punishment. The exposure was the door.
- **B. Christ is the well that answers the thirst underneath every other thirst.** In John 7:37–38 He stands and cries, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." The whole Bible ends on this same offer: "let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Revelation 22:17). Freely. The one thing your cisterns could never do, He does for nothing, at the well, at your worst hour. He went where He did not have to go, and He is still going there.

He went where He didn't have to go.

## I Am the Resurrection: The Christ Who Weeps at the Grave and Then Empties It (John 11)
*Why Jesus wept at a tomb He had already decided to open*

**Text:** John 11 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 37:1–14 · Job 19:25–26 · 1 Corinthians 15:20–26 · Romans 8:11 · Hosea 13:14 · Revelation 21:4

Jesus loved this family, and when word came that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was two more days and let him die. That is the part we skip. We want the miracle and not the delay. But John puts the delay in the record deliberately, because the sisters will throw it in His face, and He will not defend Himself. He walks to a grave four days cold, into the middle of a grief He allowed, and He does two things no one expected in that order. He weeps. And then He commands the dead to come out. The Lord of life stood at a tomb and cried, and He was going to open it the whole time.

### I. If Thou Hadst Been Here: The Delay That Looked Like Absence (John 11:1–37)

Martha meets Him on the road with the sentence both sisters had been rehearsing: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died" (John 11:21). It is not a confession of faith. It is an accusation wrapped in one. You could have come. You chose not to. And He does not correct her grief. He gives her the largest claim He has yet made about Himself. "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die" (John 11:25–26).

Notice what He does not say. He does not say, "I will perform a resurrection." He says, "I am the resurrection." The power is not a thing He wields; it is a person He is. It is the fifth of the great "I am" sayings that run through John's Gospel, the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, each one taking the divine name from the burning bush and pressing it onto a claim no mere prophet could survive making. Martha had a doctrine, "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day" (John 11:24), a correct, orthodox, cold comfort about the far future. It is exactly what a well-catechized believer says at a funeral. It is true and it is not enough, because a doctrine about the last day cannot hold your hand this afternoon. Jesus takes her doctrine and stands it up in front of her as a man on a road. The last day has a face, and it is looking at her, and it is about to ask her to believe it before she has any evidence for it at all: "Believest thou this?" (John 11:26).

- **A. He wept, the shortest verse in the Bible, and one of the deepest.** At the tomb "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). The Greek before it says He groaned in the spirit and was troubled, *embrimaomai*, a word for the snort of anger, indignation. He is not weeping in helpless sentiment. He is weeping in fury at death itself, at what sin did to the world He made, at the grave standing where a friend used to be. God incarnate hates death, and He does not hide it. He does not scold the sisters for crying. He cries with them.
- **B. His tears are not weakness in the face of what He is about to do.** The bystanders sneer, "could not this man, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died?" (John 11:37). They read the tears as impotence. But He weeps precisely because He is not indifferent to death, and He is about to prove He is not powerless over it. The tears and the miracle are not in tension. The One who will open the tomb is the One who first grieves that tombs exist at all.

### II. Lazarus, Come Forth: The Voice That Reaches Into the Grave (John 11:38–44)

He comes to the cave. He orders the stone removed. Martha, so recently confessing, panics at the smell, "Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days" (John 11:39). Four days matters. Jewish belief held that the soul departed finally by the fourth day; this was no swoon, no coma, no borderline case. This was decay. This was over. And into the mouth of a rotting tomb He prays aloud so the crowd will hear whose power this is, and then He calls one name.

"And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go" (John 11:43–44). It is worth noting that He called Lazarus by name. The old teachers said if He had not, if He had simply cried "Come forth," every grave on that hillside would have emptied at that voice. The voice that spoke the world into being in John 1, "all things were made by him", now speaks a decayed man out of the ground. This is not a healing. A healing works on the living. This is creation, the same fiat that called light out of nothing on the first morning, now calling life back into a corpse. Decay hears its Maker and obeys. There is a picture in the detail worth pausing over: the living man walks out still bound in the clothes of death, and Jesus turns to the crowd and gives them the work, loose him. The Lord raises the dead. He hands His people the folding of the graveclothes.

- **A. The word that made the world is the word that raises the dead.** Ezekiel stood in a valley of dry bones and prophesied to them, and "the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet" (Ezekiel 37:10). God asked him, "can these bones live?" (Ezekiel 37:3). At Bethany the answer walks out of a cave in graveclothes. The same *ruach*, the same word of the Lord, the same God who insists the grave is not the end of His sentence.
- **B. Lazarus was raised to die again; this was a sign, not the substance.** Lazarus came out still wrapped, still mortal, and one day he lay down and died a second time. This was a preview, not the finished work. It pointed forward to a tomb where the man who came out would leave the graveclothes folded and never taste death again. Paul names Him "the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Lazarus is the first drop. Christ is the harvest.

### III. Living Well When You Are Standing at a Grave and God Seems Late

We all have a Bethany road where we said Martha's sentence. Lord, if you had been here. The diagnosis you prayed against came anyway. The marriage you begged for died anyway. The child, the parent, the friend, gone anyway, and He could have come, and He did not. The church often answers that grief with a tidy theology about the last day, and hands the mourner Martha's cold doctrine when what they need is the face on the road. I have done it. I have offered a bereaved family the correct sentence and withheld the tears, because tears cost me something the doctrine did not.

The Christians of the first three centuries, burying their dead in the catacombs beneath Rome, scratched a strange word on the walls where the pagan tombs above them read only *vale in aeternum*, farewell forever. On the Christian graves they wrote *in pace*, in peace, at rest, as one who is asleep, and along those same corridors, in the oldest Christian art we possess, they painted Lazarus coming out of his cave again and again. It is one of the most common images in the whole catacomb of Callixtus and the others: a small wrapped figure standing at the mouth of a tomb, and a man beside it with His hand out. These believers were dying by the thousands under Nero and later under Diocletian's persecution beginning in 303, and they buried their dead as people who had read John 11. Not as those who denied the grave was real. They lived under its threat every day; they knew exactly how real it was. They buried them as those who knew whose voice would one day call into it.

- **A. The tears are permission; the resurrection is the promise.** Jesus does not shame your grief with a lecture about the resurrection. He weeps first. Christian hope was never the denial that death is terrible; it is the conviction that death is temporary. "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26). Enemy. He calls it what you feel it to be. And then He calls it defeated.
- **B. Christ is the resurrection because He walked into the grave you fear and came out.** The reason "I am the resurrection" is not a slogan is that He proved it on His own body. Lazarus was raised by a voice from outside the tomb; Jesus rose by His own life from inside it, and He never died again. Raising Lazarus is what got Him killed, the very next verses record the council resolving to put Him to death for it (John 11:53). He opened a grave, and the world sent Him to His own for it, and He walked into that one too. Romans 8:11 says "he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you." The same power that emptied His tomb is promised to yours. The book ends where every grave ends for those in Him: "and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying" (Revelation 21:4). He wept at the tomb because death is real. He opened it because He is the answer to it. And when He asks you the question He asked Martha on the road, believest thou this?, He is not asking you to deny your grief. He wept first. He is asking you to hand your grief to the only one who has ever walked out the other side of a grave.

He wept at the tomb He would open.

## The Towel and the Basin: When the Lord of All Kneels to Wash Feet (John 13)
*Why the King of glory spent His last free evening on the floor*

**Text:** John 13 · **Supporting:** Philippians 2:5–8 · Isaiah 53:2–3 · Mark 10:42–45 · 1 Peter 5:5–6 · Luke 22:24–27 · Matthew 20:28

He had hours left. The betrayer was already moving, the cross was a day away, and Jesus knew all of it. "Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father" (John 13:1). A man with that little time spends it on what matters most to him. And John tells us exactly what Jesus did with His. He got up from supper, took off His outer garment, wrapped a towel around His waist like a household slave, poured water into a basin, and knelt down to wash the dirt off twelve pairs of feet, including the two feet of the man leaving to sell Him. The Lord of all, on the floor, at the feet of Judas.

### I. He Riseth From Supper, and Took a Towel: The Descent of God (John 13:1–11)

Footwashing was the lowest job in the house. When guests arrived off the dusty roads in sandals, the task of washing their feet fell to the most menial slave, and a Jewish slave could not even be compelled to do it, it was beneath the dignity of a son of Abraham. That is the job Jesus takes. "He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself. After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet" (John 13:4–5).

Every verb is a descent. He rises only to lower Himself. He lays aside His garment, the same verb, *tithēmi*, that John uses when Jesus says of His life, "I lay it down of myself" (John 10:18). The footwashing is written to rhyme with the cross, and John means for you to hear the rhyme. Peter cannot stand it: "Lord, dost thou wash my feet?… Thou shalt never wash my feet" (John 13:6, 8). Peter's refusal sounds like humility and is actually pride, he will not be served, will not be that helpless, will not owe that much. It is easier to be the one who serves than the one who is served, because serving keeps you in control and being served admits you had a need. Jesus answers with the whole gospel in a sentence: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" (John 13:8). You do not get to keep your dignity and have Christ. There is no version of this where you clean your own feet first and then let Him shake your hand as an equal. You come to Him with dirty feet or you do not come. And Peter, in classic Peter fashion, swings to the opposite extreme, "not my feet only, but also my hands and my head" (John 13:9). He still wants to set the terms. He cannot simply receive. Neither can we.

- **A. This is Philippians 2 on its knees.** Paul writes that Christ, "being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant… and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Philippians 2:6–8). John 13 is that hymn acted out on a floor in Jerusalem. The word Paul uses, *ekenōsen*, He emptied Himself, poured Himself out, is the towel around the waist and the water into the basin. He did not empty Himself of His deity; He is fully God on that floor as surely as on the throne. He emptied Himself of the reputation, the privileges, the right to be waited on. The infinite God, folding down to the height of a household slave's work, days before folding down to the height of a criminal's cross. And Paul does not tell us this to inform us. He tells us to command us: "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 2:5). The theology is meant to end in a basin in your hands.
- **B. He washed the feet of the man who would betray Him.** Judas was in the room. Jesus knew, "for he knew who should betray him" (John 13:11), and He washed those feet anyway. He did not skip the traitor. He knelt at the feet that would walk to the chief priests and poured water over them with the same hands that would be nailed the next afternoon. This is not sentiment. This is love with its eyes open, loving the one who is already gone.

### II. If I Then Your Lord Have Washed Your Feet: The Command That Follows (John 13:12–35)

He puts His garment back on, sits down, and makes sure they understand it was not a mood. "Know ye what I have done to you? Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet" (John 13:12–14). He does not lower the title. He is Lord. He is Master. He affirms it in the same breath He tells them to imitate the basin. The greatness is real, and the greatness kneels.

This is the reversal the disciples had been fighting against for three years. Even at this table, on this night, Luke tells us they were still arguing about which of them would be greatest (Luke 22:24). Picture it, the Lord on the floor with a towel and a basin, and the men whose feet He is washing bickering above His bowed head about their rankings. That is the room. That is us. Jesus had told them plainly weeks before: "whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:27–28). The word for *minister* there, *diakoneō*, is the word for waiting tables, the lowest service. The world's ladder runs up, and everyone on it is climbing over someone. The kingdom's ladder runs down, and the man at the bottom is the King. The Son of God went all the way to the floor to show them where the throne actually was.

- **A. "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another."** He gives the mark of the whole movement, and it is not doctrine, program, or platform. "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another" (John 13:35). The watching world was never told to identify Christians by their arguments won or their influence gained. By love. By the towel. The basin is not a nice touch on discipleship. It is the identifying mark of it.
- **B. The one who serves lowest is nearest the heart of Christ.** Peter wanted to protect Jesus from lowliness because Peter still wanted a Messiah who climbed. But 1 Peter 5:5–6, written by that same man decades later, says "be clothed with humility… Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time." Clothed, the word points back to the towel around the waist. The man who refused the basin became its preacher, because he finally understood: the way up in this kingdom is down.

### III. Living Well in a Culture That Measures You by How Many Serve You

We have organized our whole world around the opposite of the basin. Status is counted by how many people work for you, wait on you, answer to you, and would drop everything at your name. We measure a life by the size of the platform and the number of the followers. And the church has caught the same fever, we build brands, chase reach, rank pastors by their arenas, and quietly wonder why the world does not believe us. I have wanted the head of the table more than the towel. I have preached servanthood from a stage designed to make me look like anything but a servant. The basin is a rebuke to me before it is an example.

In 1948, in the gutters of Calcutta, a nun left the walls of the Loreto convent, where she had taught the daughters of the comfortable in a safe and ordered religious life, and went into the worst streets in the city to pick dying strangers up off the pavement and wash them so they would not die alone and unwashed like animals. Mother Teresa spent the next half century with a basin in her hands, and when the world tried to make her a celebrity in the 1970s, she kept returning to the floor, to the sores, to the lowest work in the house. She said her sisters were doing it "to Jesus in his distressing disguise." The world called it heroism and reached for a Nobel Prize. She called it the only sensible response to a God who had washed her feet first. She had simply read John 13 and believed He meant it, believed that the Lord who knelt at the basin is still to be found on the floor, in the feet no one else will touch.

- **A. You cannot serve from a throne you refuse to leave.** The reason we struggle to wash feet is the same reason Peter struggled to have his washed, it costs us the self we are protecting. Jesus "riseth from supper" before He can serve. He had to leave the seat. Mark 10:43 is not a suggestion for the unusually humble: "whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister." Will be great. The greatness is granted. It is granted on the floor.
- **B. Christ served you all the way to the cross, and that is why you can kneel.** You do not wash feet to earn a place at the table. He said the opposite: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." He served you first, at the basin and then at the cross, and every act of service you offer is downstream of the One who washed you when you were the betrayer in the room. Read the room again, Judas was there, and Jesus washed him. Which means the towel was not a reward for the deserving. It was grace poured over the feet of a man already walking away. The only way you will ever kneel to serve someone who has not earned it is to remember that this is precisely what He did for you, on this night and on the next afternoon. The towel He wore was a rehearsal for the nails. The Lord of all knelt, and He is not ashamed of the floor.

The throne was a basin.

## It Is Finished: Why the Cross Is a Victory to Announce, Not a Defeat to Reverse (John 19–20)
*What the King meant by His last word before He bowed His head*

**Text:** John 19–20 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:5–6 · Colossians 2:14–15 · Hebrews 10:11–14 · Psalm 22:1–18 · 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 · Romans 4:25

They thought they had beaten Him. The council that condemned Him, the crowd that screamed for Barabbas, the soldiers who gambled for His coat, the powers behind all of it, they read the cross as their victory and His end. John tells the story so you cannot possibly read it their way. In John's Gospel Jesus is never a victim swept along by events. He is a King walking to a throne shaped like a cross, in full command of every step, and His last word from it is not a whimper of defeat. It is a shout of completion. He did not die because the darkness finally won. He died because the work was done.

### I. Behold the Man: The King Who Was in Command of His Own Death (John 19:1–30)

Pilate thinks he is in charge. He is not, and Jesus tells him so: "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above" (John 19:11). Pilate brings Jesus out scourged and crowned with thorns and says, "Behold the man" (John 19:5), meaning to mock Him, and speaks better than he knows. This is the man, the true man, the last Adam, the one going willingly where the first Adam ran. John keeps showing you the control. Jesus carries His own cross (John 19:17). Jesus arranges for His mother's care from the cross (John 19:26–27). Nothing is happening to Him that He has not chosen.

Then, at the end, one word in the Greek, *tetelestai*. "It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost" (John 19:30). It is a single word in the original, and it was not a specially religious word. Archaeologists have found it written across ordinary business documents of the era. Merchants wrote it across a bill: *paid in full*. Servants reported it to masters: *the task is complete*. A runner finishing a race would say it. It is not the groan of a man overwhelmed by his circumstances. It is the announcement of a workman who has finished the job He came to do. And notice the order John gives, because he gives it deliberately: He bowed His head, then gave up the ghost. Every other crucified man's head dropped because he died. This one died because He chose to, after He had lowered His head. He completed the work, bowed His head as a man lies down to sleep, and handed over His life. The verb John uses, *paredōken*, He gave it over, He delivered it up. No one took it from Him. He gave it. He said as much before it ever happened: "No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself" (John 10:18).

- **A. The debt was not reduced or excused; it was paid.** Paul says God took "the handwriting of ordinances that was against us… and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross" (Colossians 2:14). The record of debt, your record, was not torn up in a gesture. It was nailed to Him and satisfied. Isaiah saw it seven centuries early: "he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities… and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:5–6). Laid on Him. Not overlooked. Transferred and paid.
- **B. The cross is a disarming of the powers, not a surrender to them.** Colossians 2:15 says on that same cross He "spoiled principalities and powers… triumphing over them in it." In it. The instrument of His apparent defeat is the instrument of His actual triumph. The powers that thought they were nailing Him down were being publicly stripped by the man they were nailing. Hebrews 10:12 makes the finality plain: after His one sacrifice He "sat down on the right hand of God." The priests of the old order never sat, because the work was never done. He sat down. Finished means finished.

### II. The First Day of the Week: The Empty Tomb That Announced the Verdict (John 20:1–29)

If the cross were a defeat, the story would end at the tomb. It does not. "The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away" (John 20:1). John and Peter run to the grave and find it empty, the graveclothes lying there, and the napkin that had been about His head "wrapped together in a place by itself" (John 20:7). A robbed grave is chaos. This grave is orderly, the clothes left as though the body had simply passed through them. No one stole Him. He rose.

Mary stands weeping outside, mistakes Him for the gardener, and John, who has been telling us since chapter 1 that this is the Maker of a garden the first man was placed in, surely knows what he is doing letting her think so, and then He says one word. Her name. "Jesus saith unto her, Mary" (John 20:16). The same voice that called Lazarus out of the grave now calls a weeping woman by name outside His own empty one, and she knows Him instantly, the way the sheep in chapter 10 know the shepherd's voice. And to Thomas, who would not believe without the wounds, He does not scold from a distance; He comes back a week later and offers the very scars: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing" (John 20:27). The risen body still bears the marks of the cross. He could have risen unblemished. He kept the wounds. The victory did not erase them. It vindicated them, and He carries them still, forever, as the receipt of what love cost.

- **A. The resurrection is God's public verdict on the finished work.** Paul compresses the whole gospel into this: "Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and… he was buried, and… he rose again the third day according to the scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). And Romans 4:25 tells you what the rising means: He "was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification." The cross paid the debt; the empty tomb is the receipt. God raised Him to declare, in front of the whole watching universe, that the payment cleared.
- **B. Thomas moves from doubt to the highest confession in the Gospel.** The man who demanded evidence, given it, falls and says "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). John wrote none of this to win an argument for its own sake. He tells you his purpose plainly: "these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name" (John 20:31). The empty tomb is not a puzzle to be solved. It is a person to be trusted.

### III. Living Well When You Are Sure the Story Ends at the Grave

We are a people who have decided the cross is the end. Not the historical cross, the personal ones. The diagnosis that will not turn. The failure that defines you now. The death that took the person your life was organized around. We stand at those graves certain that the darkness has had the last word, and we build careful, resigned lives on the assumption that it did. I have counseled people to make peace with a grave that God had already decided to open. I have grieved as one without hope and called it realism. John 19 and 20 do not offer optimism. They offer a verdict already rendered.

In the year 250, the emperor Decius issued an edict requiring every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice to the Roman gods and produce a certificate proving it, on pain of death. The astonishing thing to the pagan world was how the Christians met the arena. They did not flee death; a great many of them walked toward it singing. When the aged bishop Polycarp of Smyrna had been ordered a century earlier to curse Christ and go free, he answered, "Eighty and six years have I served him, and he never did me any wrong: how then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?", and he went to the fire. The Roman authorities could not comprehend it, and the physician Galen, writing around the same period, noted with bafflement the Christians' "contempt of death." What Rome slowly grasped, over the two centuries until Constantine's edict of toleration in 313, was that you cannot ultimately threaten with death a people who believe death has already been beaten. The empire's chief weapon was the grave. And these people had read John 20. The grave was empty, so the threat was hollow. That conviction, held not by scholars but by ordinary believers dying in provincial arenas, outlasted the empire that killed them.

- **A. "It is finished" means there is nothing left for you to add.** The exhausting part of most religion, and most of what passes for it inside the church, is the sense that the work is never done, that you must keep paying, keep proving, keep climbing, keep earning back the acceptance you are sure you have spent. It is the treadmill Nicodemus was on and the Pharisee in the temple was on and I have been on from a pulpit, preaching grace on Sunday and living by the ledger on Monday. *Tetelestai* ends the treadmill. Hebrews contrasts the old priests, who "standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins" (Hebrews 10:11), with this One who "after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down" (Hebrews 10:12). They stood because they were never finished. He sat because He was. "By one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified" (Hebrews 10:14). Perfected. For ever. You cannot finish a finished work. You can only rest in it, or exhaust yourself refusing to.
- **B. Christ turned the worst thing into the throne, and He can do it with yours.** The connection John hands you is unmistakable, the instrument of death became the seat of the King. That is the pattern of everything He touches. He does not merely reverse the graves in your life; He announces that in Him they are already answered. The last enemy has a date on its defeat, and that date is behind us, on a hill outside Jerusalem, on the first day of a week that never ended. He bowed His head and said it was done. Then He got up.

Finished, and then He rose.
